newsitem.title: INDIA: Survivors recount horror of Indian train crash.
newsitem.headline: Survivors recount horror of Indian train crash.

text.p: Survivors of India's weekend train crash, which killed 12 people and injured 82, told of nightmarish scenes as they lay in the darkness waiting for help.
"I was trapped under a berth in my compartment and cried out for nearly half an hour before help arrived," said Babu Ram Kakkar, 57, both of whose legs suffered multiple fractures.
Kakkar was lying on Monday in a small local hospital, where 52 of the victims of Sunday night's smash were squeezed, some of them lying on cots laid out in corridors.
Many of the victims were on their way to Hindu pilgrimages.
Feroz Khan, one of the first to reach the site after the Karnataka Express collided with another train, said he helped dozens of trapped passengers get out of wreckage.
"I heard a deafening roar, there were some electrical sparks and then absolute darkness and silence," Khan said.

The Express, running 12 hours late from Bangalore to New Delhi, had collided with the slower moving Himsagar Express running from India's southernmost point, Kanyakumari, to Jammu, in the Himalayan state of Jammu and Kashmir.

Chandra Mohan, 45, one of the survivors, said: "I heard an ear-shattering noise of metal hitting metal and then I fell down from my berth. Our wagon got derailed and was sliding on the land for nearly 50 to 60 metres before it stopped."
Mohan, going from Coimbatore in the southern state of Tamil Nadu to Jammu in the north, was lying in the corridor of the Badshah Khan hospital.
The shirt of the Hindu pilgrim, on his way to a Himalayan cave-temple at Amarnath, was stained with blood.
Babloo Thakur, who was travelling more than 1,000 km (625 miles) north on a pilgrimage to the holy shrine of Vaishno Devi, said he had been in agony.
"I was crying with pain. I never had time to wait and look at the fate of other passengers," he said.
Local resident Rakesh Gambhir said relief workers had to make do with candles and small torches.
"We consoled the injured and gave them water to drink and biscuits or whatever we could get to eat. They were all screaming or crying," Gambhir said.
Ramesh Chand, 52, with his head and left hand bandaged, said: "I thought it was either a massive land slide or some sort of a volcano."
Chand was on his way to the shrine of Vaishno Devi. "Mother Goddess did not want me to come this time. Never mind. I will go again, this time hale and hearty."
